speechtext:
There was talk of building a national highway from, Montreal through Soulanges, Vau-dreuil, Jacques Cartier and the neighbouring counties, to Ottawa, and from Ottawa to Toronto. There is an urgent call for that highway. The Government have built up the eastern national highway from Montreal to Quebec, a magnificent road, and now we must have the western national highway. The Government are congratulated, and rightly so, for having built an immense military hospital in the county of Jacques Cartier, in the parish of St. Ann's, opposite the famous McDonald College. There was also an urgent need for that hospital. It is an immense building, indispensable for the welfare of the returned soldiers, the wounded the lame and the disabled; in a word, it is a national hospital. But the soldiers, the wounded and all the medical staff there, are recruited from every part of the country, from Ontario, from the Maritime Provinces and from the South. If there were a national highway from Montreal to Toronto, the relations and friends of those people would take more frequent -trips to this hospital and would profit by those occasions to see what is going on at the great McDonald school which its former owner. Sir W. C. McDonald, built at a cost of millions and millions.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if, instead of using the people's money to help out the shareholders of the Grand Trunk, the Government would contribute towards building -those great national highways, what good we could -do! We would then have an interprovincial highway, and what great advantage it

that all this should happen, because it was Government property.	>
What will be the deficit in next year's budget, as a result of the acquisition of the Grand Trunk? I am afraid it will be enormous. If the hon. gentlemen think that I am in error, let them show it; but I now think, myself, that I .am right, and that it is impossible for the State to operate a railway with any measure of success. Take the municipal corporations. They make all .sorts of by-laws, they try in every possible way to safeguard the people's money, and yet their efforts in that direction are crowned with failure. Why? Because it is public property. They spend all they can, they save nothing, and as a result, deficits .are piled up. Men act in good faith, men are honest. They have no intention to defraud or to rob, but such is their nature that when they have no direct interest they become careless, and we shall have an instance of that when this road becomes the property of the State. Consult business imen, men of experience who have made a success of their own private business; they will tell you they are against this transaction. Would they not be in favour of it if it were really a safe proposition? There are gentlemen in this House who know what work means, who spent their life working regularly and conscientiously, having not a minute of their time to spend for pleasure. They are also opposed to this transaction as being absolutely wrong. The hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. DMcC.rea) is not the first comer in this House, and I have noted what he said. He got rich through hard work, economy and good management. I know him well, he is a Scotchman, he is independent, and once he gets into his head an idea which he thinks is good, it is useless to try and make him change his mind. Now, here is what the hon. member for Sherbrooke said about the transaction:	"Mr. (Speaker, I cannot
conceive bow free men like the hon. gentlemen sitting on your right can entertain an idea of that kind."
Those men have spent their lives in business .and their judgment is most worthy of our consideration. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, if, with respect to a business question like this, I should not defer to their opinion rather than to the opinion of a lawyer? What does the hon. Minister of the Interior know about railways? Let me ask him, with all due deference, what does he know about the management of a

business of that kind? Like myself, he can see the wheels turn, he can see the trains stop at stations, he can see them run, but we are now talking about a transaction which we have to appreciate according to its proper merits, and I should rather depend upon the experience of business men for a notion of what this proposition really means.
When a working man is at work it may seem that anybodu could do his work as easily as he does it himself, but if you try your hand at that work you may alter your ideas. For instance when you see the farm hand holding the plough while at the same time guiding his team of horses, yon may imagine that it is very easy work, but take his place for a while and you will soon find out that there is more in it than you surmised.
Mr. Speaker, before resuming my seat, 1 may say that the ideas to which I have given expression have been submitted to this House in a much more proper manner by those who have preceded me in this debate, but I owed it to my electors to stand up here and register my most vigorous protest against this measure. In election time, we are glad, Mr. Speaker, to show our electors that we have raised out voice in their behalf, that we have taken their interests at heart., and that if our advice has not been heeded, we are not to he blamed. If unfortunately I have not succeeded in niv task, my conscience however is clear and I shall not be afraid to stand before them and claim absolution. Those brave electors of ours generally reproach us with not having voiced their feelings under such circumstances; they believe that it is sufficient for us to speak and that everybody will give heed to our advice. They are egregiously mistaken, for it is not so easy a task as they are apt, to believe.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I appeal once more to the conscience of the hon. gentlemen opposite, in behalf of the country cf my choice. I hope that they still entertain within themselves a sense of justice and that before coming to a division upon this unfortunate proposal, they will give it all the attention it deserves.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I also give thanks to the hon. gentlemen who have just listened to my remarks.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Friday, October 31.
While the McCormick resolution does not mention any particular railway that may become the property of the Dominion Government, the Illinois -Senator said the object was to deal with the situation that presented itself in connection with the action of the Canadian Par liament in passing a Bill to acquire possession of the Grand Trunk System.
I shall not read the rest of the article except the closing paragraph:
Congress has always been jealous of foreign control of any corporations, especially involving means of communication in this country, and special legislation has been enacted in recent years against the ownership of the majority stock of domestic corporations by alien interests. Similar legislation has been enacted against the ownership of land by aliens.
These laws may be held applicable to the Grand Trunk case, and it is not considered improbable that opposition would be aroused against retention of control of the 1,500 miles of track by the Canadian Government.

I submit that the article suggests an entirely reasonable attitude on the part of the United States. Imagine the proposition reversed. Imagine, as I have said, that we were learning for the first time that the Government of the United States was about to take over the Grand Trunk Railway system in this country and operate it, would we be indifferent to the transaction? Would the Parliament of Canada view with indifference the Government of the United States coming into this country and owning and operating a railway system within it? If we ourselves would take up a matter of that kind in a serious way have we not every reason to believe that the Government of the United States will be actuated by the same kind of motives in protecting the interests of their citizens? And if there is reason to believe that this question is likely to be one which will involve the two countries in, at least international negotiations, if not international complications, is it not the part of wisdom that these negotiations should be carried out before this matter is finally consummated, and that this Parliament should have a direct assurance recorded in the agreement which is to be drawn between the Grand Trunk Railway company and the Government that any embarrassment, or the possibility of any embarrassment between the two countries will not result from that transaction.
Now, Sir, not only is the agreement important from the point of view of the dtaount concerned and from the point of view of the properties concerned, but the principle which is involved is perhaps the most important and far-reaching of any which this Parliament will be called upon to discuss. I submit, Sir, that so far in this debate we have been unable to discover that this measure is entitled to be correctly viewed as a measure of government ownership and control. The most that we can say about it is, that from certain aspects it is a measure of government ownership; from other aspects it is certainly a measure of private ownership because the greater part of the stock remains in the hands of the private shareholders. It is a measure of transfer of control in the management of the Grand Trunk Railway Company to a commission appointed by the Government to administer the national railways; but as one hon. member this afternoon well said, the measure, in the form in which it has been drafted and brought down, presents the combined defects of government owner-

ship and private ownership and omits the virtues which belong to either of these methods of control separately exercised. I think the member to whom I refer spoke of the measure as amphibious on account of its being neither one thing mo-r the other. I think we might with equal appropriateness describe it as a hybrid affair; it is in part government ownership, it is in part private ownership but, as I have said, it lacks the value or the merit of real government ownership and has its defects. Those who advocate government ownership do so because they believe that they are getting rid of operation for the sake of profit, and securing cost. In order words they seek to get rid of paying out dividends to private sbadeholders, and through the possession of a property by public ownership seek to reserve for the public the moneys which -would otherwise be payable in dividends so that the benefit of the undertaking may go to the public in a reduction of rates. But this measure perpetuates the payments to private shareholders. It guarantees payments which, at the present time and in the past, have not been made, and so much-merit as a government ownership scheme in the truest sense would have is lacking altogether in this particular measure. Private ownership has the advantage that it stimulates watchfulness in management. The shareholders, from the fact that their returns are dependent on the efficiency of management, take an interest in the working of a concern and see that it is carried on in the most efficient way. By thlis measure all that incentive is taken away. The Government guarantees to the shareholders the dividends that they are to receive, and their interest in watching the undertaking from the point of view of efficiency in management is entirely gone. So we say that in a transaction of this kind, where the whole matter is as uncertain and doubtful in its particulars as this measure appears to be, there is the strongest reason why we should see the agreement that is about to be drafted and learn whether in as many particulars as possible it safeguards the public interest.
Indeed, I should like to suggest, Mr. Speaker, in regard to this measure that we may well pause, having in view the experience of the world in the matter of railway management, and ask ourselves the question whether it is best to jump from a monopoly of control on the part of capital to a monopoly of control on the part of the

state or whether it is not possible to work out some plan which will have fuller regard for all the interests which are involved in great industrial concerns. Looking at the United States and its management of railways we find that under Government control there the scheme has failed lamentably as a solution of the problem of rates or costs, of benefits to the consumers or to the public. Looking at the experience of England we see that the Government management of roads there has not been a success in any way towards solving the difficult problems of the relations of the parties to industry that are very certain to arise in these big undertakings. The strikes on the railway systems in England a few weeks ago showed clearly that under a system of monopoly of control by the state, when a great body of workmen went out, there was a condition which put the labour forces of the country in an attitude of apparent hostility to the government of the country as a whole and laid the basis of what might seem to be a great class war.
Now, with these examples before Parliament, is it wise to plunge into a scheme which seems to present such possibilities, without considering more carefully and in detail whether, instead of thus seeking to get rid of a monopoly of control by capital by establishing a monopoly of control on the part of the state, we might not work out some system of joint control whereby the interests of capital, and of labour, and of the state would be more effectively conserved with greater benefit to all concerned? I submit that while no one scheme could be worked out quickly, through the submission to Parliament of an agreement such as might be drafted in accordance with this principle there would be opportunity for suggestions that might be of lasting benefit to all parties concerned.
My hon. friends opposite have repeatedly said that we on this side have had no alternative to offer. Well, if we have had no alternative it has been, perhaps, because we have sought to follow advice we are giving, and not rush 'into any half-baked scheme without giving a matter of such enormous importance the careful consideration that it deserves. It would be most unwise for any body of men to seak to offer, on the spur of the moment, a scheme which has for its purpose the solution of the railway problems of the country. The only proper way to approach a subject of this kind is to permit as much as possible in the way of debate and to allow as much as possible
in the way of expressed opinion on the part of the public.
For that reason, Mr. Speaker, now that the Government have determined to go on with this measure and to enter into this contract, we hope that they will at least pause to this extent: That while proceeding at once with the agreement, they will give the public the assurance that when the agreement is drawn they will submit it to Parliament so that the people will have an opportunity of knowing the degree to which they are being bound and of expressing themselves upon it before they are committed to it for all time.
Sir, that course is necessary and desirable for the reasons that I have mentioned-the enormous size of the transaction, the vastness and complexity [DOT] of the undertaking, and the great significance of the principle involved. It is also desirable, when you stop to consider the extent of the liabilities which we are immediately assuming at a time when we are finding it extremely difficult to raise the money necessary to the carrying on of the ordinary business of the country. At this moment an effort is being made by the Government to raise a loan of $390,000,000 to meet current expenses. I wonder if it is appreciated throughout the country that every cent of that money has already been borrowed from the banks and that every cent of the loan will simply go to pay back the bankers who have been advancing money to hon. gentlemen opposite for the carrying on of the business of the country? We are told that in order to meet existing obligations, to say nothing of new obligations, we shall soon have to go again to the people and asTi for another loan of three hundred odd millions. Well, in the face of that situation, with that knowledge and that information before us, why should this particular moment of all moments be chosen to saddle upon the taxpayers of this country additional liabilities amounting to many millions.
Another reason why this agreement, when it is drafted, should be submitted to Parliament is that apparently the Government are unwilling to allow the award of the Board of Arbitrators respecting the value of certain of the stocks to be submitted to Parliament for ratification. As I have already pointed out, the stocks involved in this transaction are of two kinds. First, there are the interest stocks, amounting to $216,207,138, on which there is to be an annual interest payment of $9,500,000. That, we know, we shall have to meet; that much

is certain knowledge. But in addition to thalt there are dividend stocks amounting to $180,424,325. Now, what these stocks are worth we do not know. All that we know is that they are to be submitted to arbitration; thalt arbitrators are to give a value to them and that when they are valued the Government is to give to the holders of these stocks certificates equivalent in value to the valuation which is placed upon them by the Board of Arbitrators. We have no information, we have not been table to get from the Government any information, as to the basis on which that valuation is to proceed. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the agreement which is to be drawn between the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the Government should contain the basis on which that valuation is to be made. We do not know whether it is to be on the basis of the market value of the stocks at a given time, and, if so, what that given time may be. We do not know whether it is to be on the physical assets of the company, and, if so, whether it is to be on the basis of what it would cost to reproduce the system to-day, having regard to the increased cost of labour and material, or on the basis of the cost at the time the road was constructed. We have nothing to indicate to what extent the possible or prospective increment is to be taken into account in giving a valuation to these stocks. Sir, the amount to which this country will become liable will depend in direct ratio upon what is stipulated in the agreement in these particulars. If the Government are unwilling, as I understand they are, to refer to Parliament for its approval The valuation to be placed upon these stocks by the Board of Arbitrators, they should be at least willing to submit to Parliament the agreement between the Grand Trunk Railway Company and itself in which will be set forth the basis on which this award is to be made. It is for that reason, among others, that I urge as strongly as I can that this agreement be made subject to ratification by Parliament.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have pointed out that from a legal point of view it is unwise to suggest the submission of a certain proposition to a board of arbitrators and then ask for the right to pass upon the award. Well, I am ready to go so far as to say that if the Government are prepared to submit this agreement to Parliament so that Parliament will know on what basis this valuation is to take place, so that Parliament will be able to make at least some estimate of the amount to which the country 
is to be committed for all time, there would be strong reason for not urging that the award of the arbitrators be submitted to Parliament for its approval. But in the absence of an assurance of that kind, when a contract involving the vast sums which this contract involves is about to be entered into, it seems to me that as trustees of the people it is not merely our right, it is our duty, to surround the transaction with every precaution which it is possible for us to devise.
I wish to direct the attention of hon. members to a further reason which will, I am sure, appeal to every member of the House irrespective of the party to which he belongs. The Bill as drafted gives to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company the right to call a special meeting for the purpose of approving the agreement between the company and the Government If it is a right and proper thing to permit the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company to pass upon an agreement entered into between the Government and that company, it is equally proper and equally necessary that the same right be given to the Canadian taxpayers through their representatives in this Parliament.
It is a tendency of human nature to be very generous when dealing with other people's money, a little more generous than one often is when dealing with one's own. Another tendency very often met with is to do for others what one is not prepared to do for one's own people. We find that sometimes in individual homes; men are ready to go outside of their homes and do more for others than they will do for their own families. If there is to be charity at all, let us remember the old maxim: " Charity begins at home." No one on this side has advocated that there should be anything other than absolute fairness and justice as between the shareholders in England and the taxpayers in this country, but what we claim is that each is entitled to the same measure and method of treatment. If a stranger had visited the galleries of this House without knowing the nature of the assembly or the debate that was going on, he would very soon have gathered the impression that sitting on the Government benches opposite were directors of the Grand Trunk Railway Company defending the interests of the shareholders across the sea, and that on this side were representatives of the people of Canada looking after their interests. I would say further that if the Government persists in refusing to give to the taxpayers of Canada the same rights

as they give to the English shareholders, not merely the stranger in the gallery, but the people throughout this Dominion from one end to the other will have reason to believe that such is the case.
A great deal has been said by hon. gentlemen opposite in regard to the widows and orphans in the Old Country who are going to suffer unless the arbitration goes, as the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) himself has suggested, in a generous way for the shareholders on the other side. I do not wish to add anything to the " widow and orphan " argument excepting to point out that, while hon. gentlemen opposite have been careful to speak about the widows and orphans in England, they have forgotten to mention that after all there are only a comparatively few widows and orphans who hold shares in the Grand Trunk Railway Company, but amongst the taxpayers of this country, who are the other party to this transaction, there is not a widow nor an orphan in the whole Dominion who will not have to pay some part of the cost of this transaction. I would also like to point out that while a great deal has been said by hon. gentlemen opposite of the widows and orphans in the Old Country, they have said nothing whatever about the speculators whom the hon. member for York South (Mr. W. F. Maclean) spoke of yesterday as sweating the King's coinage and who hold some of the stock of this company. They have said nothing about the plutocrats and aristocrats who are holding privileged positions on account of being able to draw dividends, whether provided by governments or otherwise. Therefore, in this particular we can well afford to drop out of account consideration of who are the holders and who are not the holders of this stock. It woud be interesting, however, and of advantage to hon. members and to the people of this country to know -who were holding stock in this company when this matter came before Parliament first and who have secured stock since. That might throw a great deal of light on the haste with which the Government are proceeding in connection with this measure. But apart from whoever those persons may be, there is only one basis on which any board of arbitration is justified in dealing with this matter, and that is to deal with it on the basis of what is right irrespective of who the parties may be, and of giving to the people of this country the same rights as are reserved to the shareholders of the company.
I ask hon. gentlemen opposite-and I appeal to them as representatives from their
different constituencies of the people ot Canada-in considering this amendment to think of their responsibility to the people as the other party to this transaction. The Board of Directors of the Grand Trunk Railway Company have been thinking of the shareholders; in drawing up this agreement with the Government, they have been emphasizing the interest of the shareholders. We have an opportunity in this Parliament on this side of the water to stand up for the taxpayers of this country; the first duty of every member of Parliament is to protect the interest of his constituents, and there is not a man in this House who can for a moment feel that he is doing other than his duty by his constituents in advocating that the agreement should be submitted to Parliament in order that the people of Canada may have exactly the same rights in the matter of the ultimate approval of the agree-* ment as the shareholders have.
A course of that kind would be a great strength to the Government in drafting the agreement. I am sure that when the Minister of Railways and the Minister of the Interior meet Sir Alfred Smithers and the gentlemen associated with him they are continually confronted in the course of their transactions with the remark: Yes, yes, we would be glad to do this and to do that; but we have to think of the shareholders; we have to remember that this agreement when drafted will go back and be submitted to a special meeting of the shareholders, and that it must be ratified there, and while we would like to proceed in such a way, we cannot do that in virtue of the fact that the agreement must be submitted to them for ratification. It would be a great help to my hon. friends to be able to reply to Sir Alfred Smithers that they too have to consider the fact that the agreemelit has to be brought before Parliament and the people of this country. Having that position and being strengthened in it, they will certainly as a result of it effect a bargain which will be better for the people of this country and at any rate one which will have more of the confidence of the people behind it.
Just to conclude this part of my argument, I would^ again submit that that is the only right and proper method of dealing with trust funds. After all, the ministry is not handling its own money; it is dealing with the money of the people of this country, and that is something that I am afraid hon. gentlemen opposite some-

times forget. They go through with a great transaction of this kind without ever considering that the funds involved are not funds that belong to them, but funds that belong to the people of this country; that for the time being they are honoured and entrusted with the position of trustees. Therefore, I urge them to rise to the occasion as their great opportunity and to meet their position of trusteeship in the way in which it would be met in the every day walks of life. There is not a member in this House who would be willing ini a transaction-I do not care how small you like to make it, the purchase of a house or a farm-to leave to the other party in the transaction the approval or disapproval of the agreement drawn and deprive himself of an equal right. Therefore, I say to hon. gentlemen opposite: In the discharge of your public duties, be actuated by the same motives that you would be actuated by in handling your private affairs.
If that disposes' of the argument on the score of this being a business transaction, let me now appeal on the ground of what is due to PaT'iament. Let me appeal +o hon. gentlemen opposite to uphold the rights and duties and obligations of Parliament. May I remind them that the execu-except what it derives from Parliament, that it has nc authority and no rights except what it derives from Parliament, any more than Parliament has any rights and powers except those it derives from the people. So I say to the ministry. Inasmuch as we stand here as the representatives of the people and as you stand there deriving your authority from this House and this Parliament, yon should come back with this agreement when it is drawn and submit it to the people's representatives for their approval and ratification, just as the directors of the Grand Trunk will submit it to the shareholders of the company.
Sir, the war has had the effect of producing two tendencies that are all too obvious in the method by which the Government is proceeding, and has got into the habit of proceeding. There are two tendencies which war produces: one is to do everything in haste and the other is to do everything, as far as possible, by independent executive authority with as little reference to other sources as possible. Those methods may be excusable in times of war; they may be more than excusable, they may be necessary. But they are neither excusable nor necessary when you get out of times of war into times of peace, and it is

desirable that any of these habits into which the ministry may have fallen in the last four years through force of circumstances should be abandoned as quickly as possible, and that we should get back again to the normal method of proceeding, conserving to Parliament the rights which are the most highly prized of all that Parliament possesses.
Take this session as an example, if you will, in regard to both these tendencies. The session was called to deal with the Peace Treaty. Why, before the Peace Treaty was distributed, this House was told that it was a matter of such great urgency that we must proceed with it at once, that hon. members must give their final pronouncement upon it without having had the opportunity to peruse it carefully. What have we seen? Long after this Parliament bad disposed of its part in ratifying the Peace Treaty, along comes England, then France, and Italy, the great European nations that were involved in the war, to do their part in ratifying the Treaty. Even they did not feel the urgency and the haste which this Parliament exhibited. Here the Treaty was brought down and had to be dealt with hurriedly and gotten through with expeditiously at all costs. We have this Grand Trunk legislation before us now. To-morrow we will have possibly the Bill dealing with the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, and what position are we in? Already there has been introduced into the House a form of closure in morning sittings, which have always been one means of bring|ing Parliament to an end.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen may laugh, but I would ask them what other reason is there for morning sittings unless they are intended to bring the session of Parliament to a final termination? So the answer we received from the Government when we asked for time to deliberate this measure was the introduction of morning sittings, which is a form of closure, in order to shut off further discussion on this transaction,
I would further point out that when the Government brought down the Treaty they brought it down to all intents and purposes, at any rate, according to the Government professions, because they believed Parliament had a duty to perform in approving it. There was a transaction which, while it related to Canada certainly in a most important way related also in very large measure to foreign conditions on, the other

side of the ocean. If it was desirable for Parliament to ratify the agreement between the Allied and Associated Powers and Germany, it is equally desirable that a transaction of this kind, which affects Canada from one end to the other and will affect the taxpayers of this country from one generation to another, should also be ratified by this Parliament. May I point out that when, under the former Administration of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the Grand Trunk was entering into an agreement with the Government in regard to the National Transcontinental railway, the Government of that day brought down the agreement, and one clause of it provided that the agreement should be submitted to Parliament and be subject to its ratification. Hon. gentlemen opposite did not follow that method when they came to deal with Mackenzie & Mann and to take over the Canadian Northern, and we all know in what dissatisfaction that whole agreement resulted. 1 would suggest to hon. gentlemen opposite that they follow at this time the better precedent, and submit the agreement to Parliament in order that it may be ratified.
When one stops to think of the extent and magnitude of this transaction, of the obligations the country is incurring, of the vastness of the princip'e involved, of the position of the shareholders in England in relation to our own Canadian taxpayers, and the like, is there not the strongest reason why the country should be as fully informed as possible on this transaction before it is finally consummated.
Public opinion has not yet had an opportunity to express itself to anything like the extent that it should on a measure of this importance. What .are three short weeks in which to consider a momentous transaction such as this? I would also draw attention to the fact that throughout this whole discussion we have not heard the voice of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden); he has been away. We have! hardly heard the voice of the Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), or of a single minister of the Crown exceut the three who spoke at the outset, the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) the Minister of the Interior (Mr. M"dghen) and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell).

You have not been able

speechtext:
I quite'admit the truth of that. I do not think any one
has, inasmuch as my hon. friend has told us that he has not been able to digest this transaction in full himself. He has repeatedly said that he is unable to say this or that. I would also draw the attention of the House to the fact that one or two members on the other side have told the House that when they got up to speak on this transaction the minister frowned on them and they were led to believe they were not to speak on a measure of this kind. I submit that that is not the proper attitude for members of Parliament in discussing a measure of this kind.
Just one word more. Hon. gentlemen opposite have been fond of saying on different occasions that they have had a mandate to do .a particular thing. In the days when they were in Opposition they were fond of saying to the Government in power. "You have no mandate from the people. You should not go on". I ask them if they had any mandate on this measure. There has been no mandate whatever for this Government to proceed with this particular transaction. This Parliament was elected in refe ence to the winning of the war, and this session was called in reference to the Treaty of Peace. Both of these objects have been fulfilled, and now the Government, without submitting any particulars of this transaction to the people until, not the eleventh hour, but within five minutes of the twelfth hour, proceed to rush this measure through at all costs.
The Minister of the Interior the other evening, when the proposal was put before the House that the award of the arbitrators should he subject to the final approval by Parliament, said that was a. Bolshevist proposal. Let me tell him that he is mistaken as to the origin of Bolshevism. Bolshevism has never had its origin in submitting to the people's representatives a mat er wh'ch affects the people. It has had its origin in the arbitrary acts of autocratic executives, and if he and hon. gentlemen opposite want to foster in. this country Bolshevism or movements akin to Bolshevism they will persist in arbitrary acts by their autocratic Executive forcing everything through by Order in Council and refusing to give the people's representatives in parliament the rights to which they are justly entitled.
Sir, I am only too conscious ,of the fact . that I have been unable to present this important matter in the way in which it should be presented.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

My hon.
friends say, "Hear, Hear," and for that reason. I shall ask them to ponder seriously these two .considerations when they come to east theif vote on the amendment. I appeal to them as business men who are concerned in this Parliament with great business transactions, to be just as cautious in the administration of public affairs, and just as prudent and honest as they would be in the management of their own private business. I appeal to them on the further ground, as members of parliament elected to express the will of the people in this House of Commons, and chosen by the people to keep the ministry responsible to parliament, that they consider above all else at this time their duty to make this parliament the expression of the will of the people, and to make the Executive responsible to parliament in the fullest sense of the word. I move, seconded by the hon, member for Antigonish and Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair):
That this Bill be not now read a third time but that it be recommitted to the Committee of the Whole House with instructions to amend same by adding to Section 2, the following:

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
My hon. and learned friend has fallen into the error which I am sorry to see prevailing in this House, namely, of supposing that the hon. gentlemen composing the Cabinet are furnished with an irrevocable power of attorney. This is not the case; they have no power of attorney. They are a Committee of the House,

and in all matters of real importance they should come back to the House for ratification of whatever they propose to do.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there are several reasons why we should see the agreement in connection with this transaction. The first is that, a*s I believe, the interests of the Canadian people have not been fully safeguarded in the Bill itself. While the Bill-was in Committee, I asked the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) this question: Why do you not submit to arbitration the value of the four per cent guaranteed stock? He answered me very frankly that the Government would have liked to submit it to arbitration but the company was not prepared to do so. That is a frank statement, hut it is not a satisfactory answer, because the Grand Trunk railway was absolutely unable to meet their obligations, and the Government, if they proved recalcitrant, had merely to say: We will withhold all further aid from you. And then, according to the termsof the Drayton-Acworth report, the railway would not have been able to carry on. I say, therefore, that the Government had absolutely the whip-hand in the matter, and it was for them to impose upon the railway such terms-I do not ask that they should be unjust, but such terms within the limits of justice-as they deemed necessary for the protection of the Canadian people.
Then I believe that the Government should have been willing to make the arbitration subject to submission to Parliament.
I remember when that was suggested the Minister of the Interior said:	Well, why
have an arbitration at all? I would have much preferred, had the Government decided to buy this railway, that they should have made a bargain with the railway company subject to the approval of this House rather than submit the value of its stock to arbitration, because our experience in the acquisition of the Canadian Northern was most unfortunate. We found ourselves obliged to pay, under the award of the arbitrators, some $10,000,000 for stock which Sir Henry Drayton, Mr. Acworth and Air. Smith said represented no real value or investment whatever. I would have much preferred, if we are going to have an arbitration, to have had the price of these stocks fixed and referred to the House. The Minister of the Interior said that would not be an arbitration. In one sense it would not be an arbi-tion. It w'ould be what we call in the province of Quebec an expertise. It happens quite often in a lawsuit in our province that a judge will refer a technical matter to experts. These experts will bring in their report, but the report is not necessarily adopted by the judge. The party in whose favour the report is drafted moves for the homologation or acceptance of the report while the other side moves to reject the report. With the facts that the experts have found before the court it is in a better position to judge of the matter and decide upon it Such might have been done in this case.
These aie some of the facts which lead me to ask members of this House to agree to the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Prince. After all is it not a reasonable thing? Are we not reasonable men? We should be reasonable men. I would support the amendment of my hon. friend from Prince very heartily and commend it to the wisdom and prudence of my fellow members.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had intended rising when the hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) took his seat but the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) anticipated me and I did not have that privilege. The courtesies of debate require that an address in this House delivered by one occupying the conspicuous position the leader of His Majesty's loyal Opposition shall receive at all events the attention of a reply even though that address be little more than a repetition, perhaps for the tenth time, of the same remarks uttered by himself as well as by many of his followers.
The congratulations of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House are due however to the leader of the Opposition by reason of the very manifest evidence of the determination on the part of his followers to show fidelity to his leadership-evidence that came frequently to our ears in the way of applause and which was all the more pronounced and impressive when we recall the long succession of demagogic platitudes that evoked that applause. He read a lecture which he has read, I think, every time he has stood upon his feet since he entered the House about duties to the people of members of the Government and members of this House, duties that I venture in all humility to suggest every hon. member of this House was thoroughly aware of, thoroughly conscious of, long before the House received this rather nauseating reminder from the hon. gentleman.	-
If I have one suggestion to offer to the fair rose of expectancy of His Majesty's loyal Opposition; it is that when we have a concrete subject before the House for de-

bate he would be good enough to offer some remarks which really bear upon the merits of the issue and leave out of consideration, if he possibly can, these old, hackneyed phrases " democracy " '' autocracy of executives" and all the rest of it which have no more relevancy to this discussion than were he to discuss the merits of the government of Japan.
What is his amendment? He moves in this House that the agreement which Parliament is now asked to ratify shall be hereafter again submitted to this Parliament. He tells us that unless that is done it is an exercise of autocratic power on the part of the Executive, a denial of the rights of the people, a granting to the other parties to the bargain of privileges they should not receive and a refusal to follow the wholesome precedents that have been established in days gone by. He took occasion' to call to the attention of the House one of those precedents, the action of His Majesty's Government in 1903 in introducing the Grand Trunk Pacific bargain. There are two methods, as I have pointed out more than once, by which the Government might take authority for this action from Parliament. The one method is to meet the other party to the bargain, discuss and arrive at terms, write down the letter and the sentence, have the commitment complete; and then, with hands tied and feet bound, come to Parliament and say: "Take it or leave it." That is one method. Another method is to come to Parliament, lay before Parliament the general propositions, the general principles, the basis of agreement, ask Parliament to supplement these wherever it may be necessary or wherever in the judgment of Parliament they can in fairness to the public interest be improved and then seek authority in that way. I have never known or read in this Parliament or any other of the two methods being adopted. I defy and challenge hon. gentlemen opposite to bring me an instance from this Parliament, from the British Parliament, from the American Congress or from the Parliament of any civilized state, of both being regarded as necessary.
That being so, let us come to the discussion of which is preferable. I have stated the one and I have stated the other. Now I appeal to the reasonable 'men amongst the hon. members of this House: Which do they prefer? Is there an hon. member who listens to me now who would prefer that th eGovernment, the Executive of this country, should come asking the 
authority of Parliament after the consummation of the negotiations, asking for authority after the negotiations are completed, signed and sealed, rather than to come to Parliament with the general basis .of the negotiations, with the principles of these propositions and then let Parliament try to amend or improve them as Parlia-[DOT] ment may be advised? .
Which is the better position to place Parliament in? Which is the more just to hon. members of this House? Which is the fairer to the representatives of the people? Which is the more in consonance with democratic principles? Yes, in 1903 the other course was pursued on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite, and I do not wonder that as a consequence there are hon. members of this House who to-day stand up and frankly say that though in 1903 they supported, as followers of the party of hon. gentlemen opposite, the negotiations and the transactions at that time they have since had reason to repent their course in sackcloth and ashes. They have repented it, and there is no Canadian who does not repent it. " Oh, yes," hon. gentlemen say, " just do what we did in 1903?" It is because the Government of that time did what hon. gentlemen recommended in 1903 that there is $590,000,000 of unnecessary debt hanging around the neck of this country to-day. It is because of what they did and the way they did it that we have the accumulation of disasters that hangs around us now and that demands the drastic treatment we are now presenting. " Oh, says the hon. gentleman " give us a little time. We are asked for an alternative but for the life of us we cannot tell you one. This is a half-baked proposition, that is what we have to say about it; give us a little time to bake and then we will show you what we can produce." How much time did hon. gentlemen opposite give in 1903? How much time was possible under the method they followed and which we are now recommended to follow again? We stated the substance of these proposals to Parliament a year and six months ago. We notified Parliament of our policy. We advised this country of the path we were treading and of the goal that we sought, not in general vague terms, we pointed out the destination definitely and finally. Is that statement denied? That is what we did on the 15th day of May, 1918, through the voice of the Prime Minister of Canada. That is what we repeated the _ following	session	through the	voice ^ of
the	Minister of Finance, reading
the terms line for line from commencement

to the end. Previous to that we had given, notice to the country of the difficulties that confronted the Government and we appointed a commission of experts to recommend a course	to be followed. That
commission	made	a recommendation
and its recommendation-along the lines we are following now step by step, line by line-has been before the people of the country for more than two years. What did hon. gentlemen do in 1903? How many hon. members of this House who were citizens of Canada at that time heard of the Grand Trunk Pacific deal two years befo -e it was consummated? Whoever heard it mentioned-did any one hear it mentioned one year before it was consummated? Did any one hear a notification from hon. gentlemen opposite or from any hon. gentleman who sits on the Opposition now or from any hon. member in the House six months before it was consummated. Not a voice; not a whisper; not a warning; not *a note. Did any hon. gentlemen hear, even two weeks before that agreement was brought into this House signed, and sealed and final, a single word as to what the agreement contained, or even an advice that such an agreement was in contemplation? Thht agreement was brought down on the 30th day of July, 1903, all complete. It was not half-baked, it was all baked- it was baked and burnt and crusted, On the 13th day of March, 1903, Parliament was called and the speech from the Throne' was delivered. Did the speech from the Throne even contain an intimation that a Grand Trunk Pacific bargain was to be entered into or that the Government contemplated such a policy? Was any such intimation to be found there? I have the speech before me. Can the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) enlighten me before I read it? He is one of those who complain of haste and "jamming" in connection with this legislation to-day. So does the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster)-they are all complaining about it-and all acknowledging in the very same breath that nothing unfavourable can be said about the whole transaction and apologizing for speaking as a consequence. There was some reference to transportation in the speech from the Throne in 1903, and I warn hon. gentlemen to prepare themselves until I read that reference. It brings a weird memory with it, especially when one recalls the new commission policy recommended to this House by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding). Here is the reference, here is the 108
notification that, was given to Parliament on that occasion:
The great influx of population into our Northwestern territories and the very large additional areas of fertile land which are being brought under cultivation combine to further press upon us the need for increased transportation facilities for the forwarding of our grain and other products; to the markets of the world, through Canadian channels.
Now we come to the gem:
The whole question of transportation and terminal facilities continues to occupy much attention, and my Government will immediately appoint a Commission of experienced men to report on the subject.
Who was the commission that hon. gentlemen opposite appointed in pursuance of that speech from the Throne? I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, the commission they appointed. They appointed a commission to build the National Transcontinental railway in pursuance of a signed contract brought down on the 30th day of July. They had a policy in 1903 appointing a commission, but it was confined to the speech from the Throne. In practice, the policy was to sign and seal the agreement, throw it into Parliament for a. "yes" or "no"-certainly in that case a "yes"-then go ahead and bind the country, tie it hand and foot and burden it with debt for generations; whereas instead of that they had promised us a commission of inquiry. No wonder the hon. gentleman suggests a commission to us now. They planted in 1903 the forbidden fruit of which we are now reaping the consequences, and although they promised a commission of inquiry they never gave it. They planted it and committed this country to the policy without notice, warning or notification; and now, in 1919, after a commission of the best experts this country could name has inquired fully as to what to do to extricate us from the embarrassments in which those hon. gentlemen plunged us, after one commission has been appointed they go on asserting that a policy of one commission is not enough; it diid not need a commission to tie us to these embarrassments hut it needs two commissions to get us out 'of them. They also say "Let us see the agreement later on, and if you deny us the right to look at the agreement it is an exercise of autocratic insolence and is inconsistent with what we understand by democracy." It is vain to point examples to hon. gentlemen opposite. It is vain to show them over and over again that this is the ratification; that we are the representatives of the people; that even admitting they are representatives of the people themselves-in the



modesty of his nature the leader of the Opposition assured us that he and the gentlemen around him constitute the representatives of the people ol this country-here is the Bill for ratification by these representatives of the people and for consideration and determination by them. What could be more democratic than that? If the hon. gentleman will not grant us the honour of representing the people of Canada surely he will continue, to assume that honour for himself.
He says that they represent the people, but here is a Bill for ratification by the people. Unless the people's representatives ratify it, it cannot go through; where is the absence of democracy? It is vain to point out to him that any modification that hon. members here, representatives of the people, want in this Bill can be made. If they want to put in any modification that they think fair and right and square and honourable, that can be done.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman evidently did not know what I was talking about; if he did, he is very anxious to get me off the point that I was making. I was asking him if we did not represent the people and whether in deciding on the agreement as embodied in this Bill, we were not speaking for the people of Canada. If he wants to put in some basis to submit to this Parliament, some basis that is to guide and direct and restrain and constrain the arbitrators, let him submit it; now is the time; he might just as well submit it now as at the next session. Why has he not an amendment like that? It would mean something; it would not involve a tedious repetition of what he has advanced over and over again, as does the amendment which he submits now. If he thinks that there are some principles that we should lay down for the guidance and restraint of the arbitrators, let him get up in this House and suggest those principles. It is our judgment-I have said already that it is my judgment-that the principles of equity and law by which . the arbitrators will otherwise be bound are good enough and are right and are best; that they are better than any principles that we could possibly at the moment devise. It is our belief that in the hands of the Chief Justice of the Exchequer Court of

Canada, to whom has been committed for years the determination of values as between the people of Canada on the one hand and individual owners on the other, and who has discharged that duty subject to the laws of equity and of justice that have come down through generations-it is our belief that into his hands this can well be committed, subject to those laws of equity and those principles of justice.
The hon. member says that he wants the agreement submitted here because a certain agreement was submitted in 1903. Well, I have defined the course that was pursued in 1903, and I have asked hon. membe'rs to weigh the merits of the one course as against the merits of the other. I am going to say just one thing more. When the hon. gentleman states that in no case has Parliament, after laying down the determining principles in just as great detail as Parliament desired, authorized the Government, upon those foundation principles, to build in the details that were necessary, he speaks without the faintest knowledge of history.
I have dealt with that point in this House over and over again. I have quoted statutes wherein the Government of which my hon. friend was a member did that time and again-did it in 1903, did it in 1908, did it in 1910, did it, I venture to say-I did not look at the statutes-every year during which they were in power. That is the regular course that is pursued whenever a Government comes to this Parliament for authorization and ratification first and does not choose the far less desirable way of binding and tying the feet of the country and then coming to Parliament for ratification. On many occasions that has been done. It was done in the Canadian Northern arrangements which hon. gentlemen opposite made in 1910;' done in similar-arrangements in 1908, done in similar arrangements in 1903. There is nothing new about this. There is no reason why there should be an appeal to the high principles of democracy on the part of the leader of the Opposition. Why did he not make these appeals when he was Minister of Labour in 1910 and when they might have had some effect on his leader of that day? We did not notice very much struggling then on the part of the hon. member in an effort to drive into the intellects of autocratic members of this House a proper sense of the principles of democracy. He sat by while this very thing was being done then, every year during which he was in office.
I do not suppose he noticed it; nobody did.

Two years ago, in 1917, when the Canadian Northern negotiations were before this House and the same course was pursued as is pursued to-day; when the general principles that were to be the basis of arbitration and the agreement of arbitration were laid before this Parliament for the consideration of hon. members, did the leader of the Opposition of that day rise and find fault on the ground that there was not the power to insert such details and work them out to completion? Not at all. He knew that that was the regular plan; he knew that that was always done. He knew that that plan had never been abused under his Government or under the Government then in office; had not been abused at any time in the history of the country. Was it abused in the case of the agreement that was prepared following the Bill that authorized the Canadian Northern arbitration? I had an allegation from the leader of the Opposition that it was abused. I challenged him then to make good his allegation; I challenged him to bring forward one single clause or sentence of that agreement which had been prepared on the authority and faith of the statute passed by this House and which was out of consonance with that statute, or which, in fact, did not safeguard the public rights or was a concession to the other parties to the bargain. Has he made good the allegation? He talked a lot along lines of what I must describe as demagogism, but he did not attempt to make good the specific allegations which he recklessly put forward on a subject which I venture to say he knew nothing at all about.
Now, the hon. member tells us that he is afraid we are going to get into great trouble with the United States. He read an article -no, he did not; he read part of an article -from a newspaper called The Journal of Commerce, published in New York. After reading such extracts, as suited him, he told the House that the suggestion of the article was that there would be objection to this agreement on the part of the United States Government, and that, as a consequence, he had a new reason for hesitation to advance. The article in question does comment upon the course that is being pursued. It contains, I think, exactly the extracts that he quoted; it gives one side and the other side. I do not wonder that there should be such an article, following the fears that hon. gentlemen expressed in the early part, of this debate almost a month ago now. I do not wonder that these fears would be carried by the winds and the telegraph wires down
to the United States, and that some newspaper would have an article upon them. But he took care not to read it all; he explained to the House that he would not read the rest of it and he simply let it go at that. I will read a little of the rest of it, and perhaps hon. members will then understand why he did not read the rest of it:
No similar issue has ever come before the State Department, it is understood. There is some disposition to believe that the ownership of the stock of the Panama railroad by the Government of the United States furnishes a parallel case. The statement has been made that the Panama railroad as a corporation is subject to the same control by the Pan-American Government as any other private enterprise, and it is probable that this will be the attitule of the United States as to the Grand Trunk system.
I am afraid the hon. member has sent out an invitation to a ghost that is not likely to be accepted. He has at least one bogey that he won't very often put up to knock down again.
The hon. member made some other references in the course o-f his address, many of theta nothing more or less than repeated misrepresentation of statements that had been made on the part of the Government and misrepresentations of figures that had been brought down. He went so far as to say that the House had not been advised of the obligations of the system, notwithstanding the fact that every obligation has not only been brought down, but its proper allocation made and its nature fully defined. The proper division and the various characteristics of the obligations have been amply explained.
All obligations to the last dollar are pretty well known to this House and to any hon. member who desires to peruse the papers that have been laid on the Table, and I do not know what more a Government can doi The hon. member asks then finally and as a last plea that we be good enough to bring down the agreement so that it may be seen by hon. members of this House. Most assuredly, it .will be brought down. I have never known, in all my knowledge of Parliament, of an agreement made on behalf of a Government that was not laid on the Table when it was made or just as *soon as possible afterwards. That undoubtedly will be done; but if we are not to do anything until the agreement brought down, what is the good of what we are doing now?

If after this debate the agreement is to be submitted to Parliament for review again, what is the good of this debate or of this Bill? There is no sense in taking the two courses, as the hon. member must surely see. There is no common sense nor propriety; in fact, greater lunacy could not possibly be conceived of than to take the two courses. What is the object of the debate on this Bill? This de-

bate is the method by which Parliament is made aware of the principles, indeed, the specific clauses which, so far as Parliament desires, are to be embodied in the agreement. If the agreement is later to be brought down for review, what is the good of this debate? You have to take one course or the other.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
One course or the other must be pursued. To take the two courses is simply to play with Parliament, and I cannot conceive of anything so wholly indefensible-I described it as lunacy. You could not possibly defend both courses. It is for Parliament to decide whether we are justified in taking this course or whether the other would be better. I put it to hon. gentlemen:	Do you prefer the course of
1903, or do you prefer this? Do you prefer to have something to say as to what is in the agreement, or do you prefer to have no opportunity at all except to say:	Yes or
no? That is what is before the House. Certainly the agreement will be brought down; but when a Government is authorized to make an agreement and when that Government is told the nature and the only nature which that agreement can have, then that is the authority of that Government; and that is the best method of procedure in the interest of Parliament and in deference to the just rights of Parliament and of the people whom Parliament represents. That is the best way and the democratic way to go before Parliament. It is not the 1903 method; I do not think the people of this country want the 1903 method any oftener than is unavoidable. I will tell the House a little more about that method. In 1903, the Government of the day made an agreement with the Grand Trunk Railway Company. They threw the agreement into the arena here, and do you know the way in which they did that? They did not even put a resolution on the Order Paper that hon. members in the Opposition or the hon. members behind the Government could see it and know what in the world it was before the debate came on. I said a moment ago that there was not a week's notice; I want now to tell this House that there, was not an hour's notice; that there was not a minute's notice. I will explain the procedure that was followed, a procedure, I think, unprecedented in the history of this or of any other Parliament. The leader of the Government of that day stood in his place and moved for leave to introduce a Bill. By the rules of the House there had to be a resolution before the Bill could

be committed; but he introduced the Bill before he introduced the resolution. Why: Because if he had introduced the resolution first, he would have had to put it on the Order Paper to introduce it, and then hon. members would have known what was contained in the resolution. He did not want that, so he preceded the resolution by the Bill. You do not' have to distribute the Bill. Pie got up and made a speech ol about two hours in length, and none of the members of the House had ever had the Bill before him, and when he got through with his speech, he sent across for the first time a copy of the Bill to the leader of the Opposition That is a course in the interest of democracy, il you please. That is the fidelity to democratic principles that is' solemnly advised on' the part of the leader of the Opposition to-day. We want no more of the manner or the form or the substance of the 1903 course again in this Parliament or in this country. Therefore, I say that of the two methods that were before us from which we might choose, we have chosen the one that shows the greatest consideration for members of Parliament, that gives the people of this country the best chance to be heard, that is in every way the most democratic and, indeed, the most prudent in the interest of the whole nation.

If my hon. friend would go into the office of the Nova Scotia Steel or the Dominion Coal Company he would find that a $10,000 order is a very small affair. When the traveller sells that order he says to the purchaser: "This order is not binding until my principal at home approves it. That is the kind of bargain, I am making with you, and if you do not get the goods you have no cause for complaint because you understand from the beginning I am only making a tentative bargain, which, if my principal does not approve, is no bargain at all." That is the kind of agreement we made in 1903 with the Grand Trunk. We simply said to them: "We will make this tentative agreement with you, and if Parliament approves, it will become a bargain, but if Parliament rejects it there will be no bargain at all." That is the position we took, and it is a most extraordinary thing for hon. gentlemen opposite to allege-it is an accusation

against themselves-that Parliament has absolutely no independence, and that a Government or a section of a Government can make any kind of an agreement, and if they make it that is the end of it, it being a useless formality to submit it to Parliament, because Parliament must adopt it. I do not go that far, and I hope hon. gentlemen opposite will not go that far. Are they going to strip themselves entirely of their independence and of every particle of judgment and say that if the Government which they support brings in an agreement, that is the end of it, because they must vote for it? That would be stripping Parliament of all its power; the will of the people as represented by Parliament will be a thing of the past if that is what they are going to do. I hope that none of the Unionist party, which is only a little step from old hard-and-fast Toryism, will say that that is the doctrine they espouse, and that it is carrying out the will of the people. If so, they might as well stay at home and send a rubber stamp here instead of themselves. The Minister of the Interior could then put the rubber stamp on the agreement and save them the trouble of coming here at all. But that was the doctrine put forward to-night by hon. gentlemen on the other side.
What was the practice followed in 1903? I am not going into all the details of the agreement, and I am speaking from memory, but the agreement was submitted to Parliament and approved after a very lengthy discussion; I forget how long, but it was months before Parliament had fully discussed and thrashed out the matter. Furthermore, not a dollar o"r a cent was expended under that agreement until Parliament was dissolved and the Government of the day had appealed to the country on that question. If hon. gentlemen opposite will follow that same course there will not be five minutes further discussion on this side of the House.
Mr. MEIGHE.N: Was not the Bill passed in 1903 before there was any appeal to the country, and was there not even a new contract made with the Grand Trunk which passed the House before there was an appeal to the country?

speechtext:
I say there was no
money expended, nor a sod turned on the road until after the election. I did not

come to this Parliament for the first time in my life until after the election of 1904, when I met in Ottawa for the first time one of the Commissioners who was then organizing his staff and getting ready to begin work. Not a dollar was spent on the work before the election. While it is true that the Government could possibly bind the hands of representatives of the people sitting behind them in Parliament, no Government except this Government would make any attempt to bind the hands and feet of the electorate of this country. In 1903, as the Government was entering into a great undertaking, they submitted the agreement to the people of the country and the people of the country approved it. We * cannot hope to be wiser than the great masses of the people of this country. The masses of the people, the people of the country generally, are not all wise, . but they are the best we have, and when we submit a question to their cool deliberation and judgment and they reach a verdict, we have to stand by it, and there is no use crjdng over spilt milk if we find the verdict was not exactly what we thought it might be. The ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) speaking in this House a few evenings ago said it was a waste of time to indulge in recriminations as to who was to blame for the railway situation. If there was any blame, we must share it equally, he said, and do the best we can.	*
Without taking up much time, let me say that I prefer the course that was adopted in 1903. I say to the Government, bring the Bill and the agreement before Parliament and get the approval of Parliament. But do not be satisfied with that. Submit not only the Bill and the agreement to the people of this country, but submit the Government itself to the people. If hon. gentlemen opposite are so courageous and believe they represent the will of the people in going on with this transaction, let them say to the Grand Trunk people: We are a government which was elected on a specific cry and for a specific purpose. We have never discussed this question with the country and the Canadian people have not had an opportunity of passing judgment upon it. Wait until the proper times comes, or until we make a proper time for appeal to the country. We will then make this an issue, and if the Canadian people approve of the agreement and give us a mandate to go on with the transaction, and -add this further weight of public ownership to the present burdens of the country, we shall be prepared to give

the matter serious -consideration, but until that time comes it is better to leave such an im-porant question in abeyance. I submit that that would be a business proposition and the proper way of dealing with a matter of this kind. We are not following the course that was adopted in 1903. Instead of that, a Bill is introduced in Parliament which does not profess to go into details of the various things that are to be done undeT the agreement, but simply gives a general power to the Government to do certain things. We say that that is not sufficiently specific. We say that the agreement itself, which will practically be an Act of Parliament. or a supplement to this Act, should be brought before Parliament. And when we do see it we shall possibly be ready to submit it to the proper authorities for the further carrying out of it.
Now, as to what the practice is, let hon. gentlemen look 'at Chapter 20 of the Acts of 1914 respecting the Canadian Northern railway. That Bill was drafted by my hon. friend, the Minister of the Interior, (Mr. Meighen) with some assistance no doubt; and he will admit, I think, that he had something to do also with the drafting of the present Bill before the House. In 1914 there was an agreement as well as a Bill. The agreement is part of Chapter 20 of the Acts of 1914, and every particle of it, every term and provision of the agreement, is set forth in the Bill itself. Now, if that represented good practice on that occasion by the same Government carrying into effect what they termed the government ownership of railways, what is the matter with it to-day? We are simply asking the Government to be uniform in their procedure. If I were informed by my good friend, the distinguished surgeon from Toronto, (Mr. Sheard) that he performed a certain major operation some two or three years ago in a particular way that proved highly successful, and that he intended performing the same operation again, would he for one moment, merely for the sake of experiment, adopt any practice other than that which he had already tried and found eminently satisfactory? _ Not by any means; he would do precisely as he had done before. In this matter, we are asking parliamentary practitioners, who are now practising upon the carcass of the country, to follow the practice which they themselves have already laid down. For about the hundredth time, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of the Interior tells us that this bargain was submitted to us on May 5, 1918, by the Prime Minister, and he asserts that we should have stood up in our places on that occasion and protested even against the Prime Minister's talking about the matter. But, Sir, it was nothing more nor less than general talk in regard to the railway situation. No Bill was submitted. I want hon. gentlemen opposite to be fair to this side of the House and to themselves. Why should we begin
to	criticise a Bill	that	was	notintroduced, and an	agreement '	thatwas	not . formulated	in	any	way?The	Prime -Minister at	that	time	was
dealing largely, as I venture to say, with the question of general policy in regard to the unification of railways in this country, blotting out here and there useless pieces of railroads, and devising some working arrangement to secure a co-operative basis of railway operation in Canada with a view to saving overhead expenses and carrying on the systems as satisfactorily as possible. I forget what the Prime Minister said in relation to the Grand Trunk, but, whatever it was, it was all in connection with the general discussion. The leader of the Opposition at that time, Sir Wilfrid Laur-ier, took part in the discussion and made statements in the -same general way. But, I repeat, there was nothing definite before the Government; there was nothing definite before the House. Yet we are told to-day that- we must say nothing , about this Bill because, forsooth, we -raised no objection when the mere mention of the matter was made in this House in 1918. In answer to my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior, the other evening, I drew his attention to a cablegram appearing in this blue-book, sent by the Prime Minister of Csftiada on the 10th day of September, 1918, to the Canadian High Commissioner in London, asking him to convey to Sir Alfred Smith-ers a message that unless a better proposition was submitted before the end of September, 1918, than had hitherto been made, all negotiations would have to be regarded as closed. When the Minister of the Interior says that we knew that some negotiations were in progress on the 15t-h of May, 1918, I think that the telegram of the Prime Minister on the 10th day of September should be accepted as a fair answer to the statement that we should have criticised this transaction all along. There was no offer subsequently to the 1 Oth of September, and, so far as we are concerned, that was the end of the negotiations until the 9th day of last month when the Minister of the Interior introduced this legislation. We are now told that, in the language of the law, we are

estopped from criticising the bargain because we were not barking at the heels of the Government all the time. That is not a fair or reasonable position for hon. members opposite to take, and we have a right to ask that we shall be put on the same basis exactly as those who are selling the road. The vendors are told in this Bill that they shall have the right to look at the agreement and pass judgment upon it before signing it, and we who are buying the road should also have the opportunity of seeing the agreement and assuring ourselves before signing it that it embodies every provision necessary to safeguard the interests of the people. The Minister of the Interior, although he did not make the statement to-night, has said that this attitude of inquiry on the part of the Opposition is Bolshevism. Bolshevism! For us to suggest that the people of the country, through their representatives in Parliament, should see the agreement before committing themselves to it. That point has already been adequately .dealt with, and I shall say nothing concerning it, except to remark that if , our anxiety in this House in the interests of the people, and our desire to know just how public money shall be expended;-if this, and our request for ample opportunity to ascertain what we are undertaking in the way of financial obligations, constitute Bolshevism, then all I have to say is that there are a great many Bolshevists in this country; because we do not want
